cards.title: Inquiry into action
cards.label: A letter to our learning community
cards.body:
The questions that matter most rarely stay inside a classroom. They emerge in staff meetings, community conversations, learning spaces, and the moments when familiar approaches stop working. This season, we invite our EdD community to bring those questions into conversation with one another.

Our theme is simple: listen closely, investigate thoughtfully, and share what you learn. A useful next step might be a more inclusive meeting, a sharper research question, or a new partnership shaped with—not merely for—the people it serves.

In this edition, we explore the connections between reflective practice, belonging, and public scholarship. Wherever you are in your doctoral journey, make room for a colleague’s perspective and for the possibility that your next insight will begin with a better question.
cards.author: Program leadership · demonstration message
cards.quote: What changes when we treat the people closest to a challenge as partners in understanding it?
cards.imageAlt: Two adults in conversation on a sofa; illustrative imagery from the Antioch University brand guide.

cards.title: Writing together: a focused hour
cards.label: Illustrative date · 6–7 p.m. Eastern · Online
cards.body: Bring one achievable goal: revise a paragraph, map an argument, or organize a set of research notes. Begin with a brief check-in, work quietly alongside peers, and close by naming your next step. Demonstration event; consult the Community Center for actual dates.

cards.title: Problems of practice, shared perspectives
cards.label: Illustrative date · 7–8 p.m. Eastern · Online
cards.body: A discussion-format workshop invites participants to describe a challenge from their professional setting and examine whose perspectives are represented. Leave with one question worth investigating. Demonstration event, not an announced program session.

cards.title: Dissertation conversation: from question to design
cards.label: Illustrative date · 6–7 p.m. Eastern · Online
cards.body: Explore the relationship between a research question, the evidence needed to address it, and the practical realities of gathering that evidence. Demonstration session; no defense or candidate is being announced.

cards.title: Connection is part of the work
cards.label: Community practice
cards.body:
Doctoral work can be solitary; it does not have to be isolating. Try a small peer check-in: share one idea that is taking shape, one obstacle, and one specific kind of feedback you would welcome. Listening before advising makes room for different contexts and different ways of knowing.

For your next conversation, bring an artifact of practice—a meeting agenda, a learning activity, or a question from a community partner—and ask what it reveals about participation and voice.
cards.quote: A strong learning community makes it easier to ask an unfinished question.

cards.title: The five-minute reading exchange
cards.label: Try this with a peer
cards.body: Choose one passage from a reading that challenged an assumption. In a brief exchange, explain why it stayed with you and ask your partner what it brings to mind in their own setting. Resist the urge to agree too quickly: a useful conversation can reveal where the same idea meets different realities.
cards.quote: What does this idea help us see—and what might it leave out?

cards.title: From a compelling concern to a researchable question
cards.label: The dissertation journey
cards.body:
A problem of practice begins with a concern you can describe clearly in context. Before narrowing a question, write a short account of who experiences the problem, what you currently know, and what remains uncertain.

Then consider the fit: what evidence would help answer the question, who should shape the inquiry, and what is feasible within your setting? Bring that working account to your next advising conversation. The goal is not a perfect first formulation; it is a defensible next step.

cards.title: A milestone worth recognizing
cards.label: Illustrative milestone feature
cards.body:
This space can celebrate a proposal moving forward, an approved research plan, a completed analysis, or a successful defense. For this mockup, the featured milestone is a fictional practitioner’s move from a broad interest in belonging to a focused study of how adults experience participation in team learning.

The story behind the milestone matters: careful revision, thoughtful feedback, and persistence. No actual dissertation approval or defense result is being reported.

cards.title: Arrive with a question. Leave with a connection.
cards.label: Preparing for residency
cards.body:
Residency creates an opportunity to connect sustained inquiry with shared conversation. Prepare a two-minute introduction to your current work, choose an artifact that illustrates your practice, and identify a question that would benefit from perspectives beyond your own field.

Build in time to listen, reflect, and follow up. Afterward, send one colleague a resource or question that continues the conversation. Confirm all schedules, locations, and preparation requirements through official program communications.

cards.title: Making room for every voice
cards.label: Student spotlight · fictional composite
cards.body:
In this fictional composite story, a school-based educator notices that the same few voices tend to shape professional learning meetings. Rather than assuming that silence means agreement, the practitioner begins asking how the meeting itself might influence participation.

Their developing inquiry considers reflective writing, smaller discussion groups, and opportunities to contribute before and after a meeting. The emphasis is on listening to colleagues and examining the conditions that help people participate.

The story illustrates the kind of practice-centered student feature this newsletter could carry. It does not describe a real Antioch student, study, or research finding.
cards.author: An educator’s inquiry into belonging
cards.quote: I began by asking how to improve participation. I am learning to ask who gets to define what participation looks like.

cards.title: Carrying inquiry beyond the dissertation
cards.label: Alumni connection · fictional composite
cards.body:
In this fictional alumni profile, a community-organization leader carries a reflective inquiry habit into everyday work. The team sets aside time to examine a service experience from the perspective of the people who use it, then invites those participants to help shape the next questions.

The most valuable change is not a new title or a finished report. It is a more deliberate routine: notice assumptions, seek perspectives that are missing, and make decisions that can be revisited as understanding grows.

This narrative demonstrates an alumni feature format. It is not an account of an actual graduate or an attributed professional accomplishment.
cards.author: A continuing practice of learning with others
cards.quote: The degree may end, but the responsibility to keep asking better questions continues.

cards.title: Scholarship that travels beyond the seminar
cards.label: Research & public scholarship
cards.body:
Who could use your ideas beyond an academic audience? Consider a short practice brief, a facilitated conversation, or a visual explanation that helps a community partner engage with a question. Begin with what the audience needs to understand, and make the limits of the evidence as clear as the possibilities.

Environmental learning offers one useful lens: questions about place, responsibility, and participation can bring professional practice into conversation with community priorities. The photograph is illustrative brand imagery, not documentation of an EdD research project.
cards.imageAlt: An adult standing among plants in a greenhouse, with Antioch brand graphics; illustrative image, not a featured student.

cards.title: Turn one idea into a practice brief
cards.label: An invitation to share your thinking
cards.body:
Choose a question from your professional setting and draft a one-page brief for a nonacademic audience. Describe the context, explain why the question matters, and offer one carefully qualified implication for practice. Ask a colleague outside your specialization to read it for clarity.

This is an editorial activity for the mockup, not a funded opportunity, formal call for proposals, or required assignment.

cards.title: Find the conversation your work belongs in
cards.label: Professional learning
cards.body: As you consider workshops, conferences, and community forums, look for audiences connected to your problem of practice. Review the purpose, accessibility, cost, and submission requirements before committing. A small local conversation can be as useful as a large conference when the right partners are at the table.
cards.buttonLabel: Explore university news and events coverage

cards.title: Make space for the next draft
cards.label: Writing & research support
cards.body: When writing feels stalled, separate the tasks. Use one session to clarify the claim, another to organize evidence, and a third to revise for a reader. Bring a focused question when seeking feedback: “Where does the argument become difficult to follow?” is often more useful than “Is this good?”

cards.title: Access belongs in the plan
cards.label: Resources & wellbeing
cards.body: Plan your learning with access and sustainability in mind. Protect a realistic work rhythm, identify the support you need, and use official university channels to discuss accommodations. You do not have to solve every barrier on your own.

cards.title: A little company. A little progress.
cards.label: Illustrative session · 6–7 p.m. Eastern · Online
cards.body:
Bring your writing, reading, or planning—and a cup of whatever helps you settle in. Our demonstration Café format opens with a friendly check-in, makes space for focused work, and closes with a brief reflection. You can arrive with a small goal and leave with a little momentum.

This date and time are illustrative. Confirm the actual session schedule through the Community Center before joining. The button uses the program’s supplied Café Zoom destination; no registration is required.

cards.title: Keep the conversation going
cards.label: Stay connected / Need help
cards.body:
Let the newsletter be your starting point and the Community Center your home for current program information. Return there for updates, resources, and the appropriate program contact pathways.

Have a story about your learning, practice, or community work? Prepare a short summary and confirm the program’s current submission process. Stories and photographs should be reviewed and approved before publication; this mockup does not collect submissions.
